title: No. 1 — General Introduction (Hamilton)
paragraphs: After clear and unmistakable evidence that the existing federal government does not work, you are now called upon to deliberate on a new Constitution for the United States of America. The subject speaks for its own importance. Its consequences amount to nothing less than the survival of the UNION, the safety and welfare of its component parts, and the fate of an empire that is, in many respects, the most consequential in the world. It has often been said that the people of this country seem to have been chosen, by their conduct and example, to settle a critical question: whether human societies are truly capable of building good government from reflection and choice, or whether they are forever doomed to depend on accident and force for their political constitutions. If there is any truth to that observation, the present crisis can rightly be regarded as the era when that decision must be made. A wrong choice on our part would, in this view, count as a general misfortune for all of humanity.

This idea adds the motives of philanthropy to those of patriotism, sharpening the concern that all thoughtful and decent people must feel about the outcome. We will be fortunate if our choice is guided by a sound judgment of our true interests, undisturbed and unbiased by considerations unrelated to the public good. But this is more to be hoped for than realistically expected. The plan put before us touches too many particular interests and disturbs too many local institutions not to draw in many issues unrelated to its merits, along with views, passions, and prejudices that are unfriendly to the discovery of truth.

Among the most formidable obstacles the new Constitution will face are two clearly visible ones. First, there is the obvious self-interest of a certain class of men in every State who will resist any change that might reduce the power, salary, and importance of the offices they hold under the State governments. Second, there is the perverted ambition of another class who either hope to enrich themselves through the confusion of their country, or flatter themselves with better prospects for advancement if the empire is broken into several partial confederacies rather than united under one government.

It is not, however, my plan to dwell on observations of this kind. I am well aware that it would be unfair to dismiss the opposition of any group simply because their position might invite suspicion, treating them all as motivated by self-interest or ambition. Honesty requires us to admit that even such men may act with upright intentions. There is no doubt that much of the opposition that has appeared, or may yet appear, will spring from sources that are at least blameless if not respectable—the honest mistakes of minds led astray by preconceived suspicions and fears. Indeed, the causes that bias judgment are so numerous and so powerful that on many occasions we see wise and good people on the wrong as well as the right side of questions of the highest importance to society. This fact, properly considered, would teach moderation to those who are utterly convinced they are right in any controversy. Another reason for caution is that we are not always sure that the defenders of truth are guided by purer motives than their opponents. Ambition, greed, personal hostility, party loyalty, and other motives no nobler than these are just as apt to operate in those who support the right side of a question as in those who oppose it. Even without these reasons for moderation, nothing could be more wrongheaded than the intolerant spirit that has always marked political parties. In politics, as in religion, it is equally absurd to try to make converts by fire and sword. Heresies in either field can rarely be cured by persecution.

And yet, however just these sentiments may be, we already have ample signs that this debate will follow the pattern of every great national discussion. A torrent of angry and malignant passions will be unleashed. Judging by the conduct of opposing parties, we can expect both sides to try to prove the rightness of their views, and to win converts, through the loudness of their declamations and the bitterness of their attacks. An enlightened concern for the energy and effectiveness of government will be branded as the offspring of a temperament that loves despotic power and hates liberty. Excessive anxiety about danger to the rights of the people—which is more often a fault of the head than of the heart—will be portrayed as mere pretense and trickery, the stale bait of popularity at the expense of the public good. On one hand, it will be forgotten that suspicion is the usual companion of love, and that a noble enthusiasm for liberty is liable to be infected with a narrow and illiberal distrust. On the other hand, it will be equally forgotten that the vigor of government is essential to the security of liberty; that, in the eyes of sound and well-informed judgment, their interests can never be separated; and that a dangerous ambition more often hides behind the plausible mask of zeal for the rights of the people than under the suspect appearance of zeal for firm and effective government. History will teach us that the first has been a far surer road to despotism than the second, and that of those who have overturned the liberties of republics, most began their careers by paying obsequious court to the people—starting as demagogues and ending as tyrants.

In the course of the preceding remarks, my fellow citizens, I have aimed to put you on guard against any attempts, from any quarter, to influence your decision on a matter of the utmost importance to your welfare by anything other than the evidence of truth. You will, no doubt, also have gathered from the general drift of these remarks that they come from a source not unfriendly to the new Constitution. Yes, my countrymen, I admit to you that, after careful consideration, I am clearly of the opinion that it is in your interest to adopt it. I am convinced that this is the safest course for your liberty, your dignity, and your happiness. I do not pretend to reservations I do not feel. I will not entertain you with the appearance of weighing the matter when I have already decided. I frankly tell you my convictions, and I will openly lay before you the reasons they rest on. The consciousness of good intentions disdains ambiguity. I will not, however, multiply professions on this point. My motives must remain locked in my own breast. My arguments will be open to all and may be judged by all. They will at least be offered in a spirit that will not disgrace the cause of truth.
I propose, in a series of papers, to discuss the following important particulars:

THE USEFULNESS OF THE UNION TO YOUR POLITICAL PROSPERITY; THE INADEQUACY OF THE PRESENT CONFEDERATION TO PRESERVE THAT UNION; THE NECESSITY OF A GOVERNMENT AT LEAST AS ENERGETIC AS THE ONE PROPOSED, IN ORDER TO ACHIEVE THIS OBJECT; THE CONFORMITY OF THE PROPOSED CONSTITUTION TO THE TRUE PRINCIPLES OF REPUBLICAN GOVERNMENT; ITS ANALOGY TO YOUR OWN STATE CONSTITUTION; and lastly, THE ADDITIONAL SECURITY THAT ITS ADOPTION WILL PROVIDE FOR THIS FORM OF GOVERNMENT, FOR LIBERTY, AND FOR PROPERTY.
As this discussion proceeds, I will try to give a satisfactory answer to all the objections that have appeared and that seem to merit your attention.

It may seem unnecessary to argue for the usefulness of the UNION, a point no doubt deeply engraved on the hearts of the great body of people in every State, and one that may be imagined to have no opponents. But the fact is that we already hear it whispered in the private circles of those who oppose the new Constitution: that the thirteen States cover too great an area for any single general system, and that we must inevitably resort to separate confederacies for distinct portions of the whole.(1) This doctrine will, in all probability, be gradually spread until it has enough adherents to support an open declaration of it. For nothing can be clearer, to those who are able to take a broad view of the subject, than the choice between adopting the new Constitution and dismembering the Union. It will therefore be useful to begin by examining the advantages of that Union, the certain evils, and the probable dangers, to which every State will be exposed if it is dissolved. That, accordingly, will be the subject of my next paper.
1. The same idea, traced to its consequences, is put forward in several of the recent publications against the new Constitution.
